intro: Are YOU tired of games that make sense? Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen rules, and the game has to keep every one of them. Today's roll was seed 1365651629. Here's how a firework, some moons and a 3 a.m. infomercial ended up on the same roof. But wait, there's more.

rolls.value: a fireworks who reads every manual
rolls.became: Dudley, a rocket firework who reads every manual, which is exactly why he has never once gone off. There's always another page. He reads the comb's manual (one page: COMB), the warranty's warranty and the Gala rulebook, and that last one is the whole game.

Anything that comes on a string in a box comes out tangled. Fairy lights, headphones, and, it turns out, moons. Every flick on Moon-in-a-Box tugs a few knots loose, and when the top moon's knots hit zero it flies free.

Moon-in-a-Box, 'Light up any night!', twelve moons for the price of one. Dudley needs them because of Rule 14(b) of the Rooftop Gala: you're scored on the light in the sky during your slot, and any light counts. Including moons. Nobody else read Rule 14(b).

You flick up on the box, like striking a match, and each freed moon flies where you flicked it, higher if you flicked harder. Flick a clump of moons to split it, or a single moon to nudge it about the sky.

Astrid, a Roman candle who has never read a single instruction and has won the Gala every year anyway. The meter is Dudley's moons against her sky-light, and she raises her mark with every box: 12, then 36 (the Mega Candle), then 99 (the Grand Finale Pack).
Astrid. She heckles. "Still reading, Dudley?" She's also on the testimonials, eventually.

Moons are heavy, and heavy things pull on each other. Once there are enough moons up, two of them drift together into a worried little clump, and if nobody flicks it apart it drops back into the box, tangled again. The more moons, the more pull, so it gets busier as the sky fills. Sky Hooks, Personal Space Rings and Sideways™ ("fall around it": that's what an orbit is) are how you argue with it.

rolls.value: distinct phases, each its own small economy
rolls.became: Three boxes, three little economies, one currency at a time. Box One pays in Glow: moons just hang there shining. Box Two ('But Wait, There's More!') brings a crowd to the roof, and the crowd pays in Oohs for every flick, every moon and every split. Box Three ('Call Now!') pays in Pull, the moons' own gravity, which grows faster than the number of moons and buys the Upsy-Daisy™ Lift Kit, a beam that lets the sky pull knots loose by itself.

Testimonials, the infomercial's favourite thing. Each one is a seal under the poster and makes everything pay ×1.15 more. They're from very satisfied customers: Moon #1, two moons who were too close, a Gala judge, a mouse. One of them you get by reading the labels on eight things in the shop, because of course it is.
Ninety-nine moons, and not one more. Prices stay in the tens and low hundreds. The headline number never needs a comma.
About half an hour on the roof: three boxes, each a few minutes longer than the last, and the Comb-o-Matic combing on its own from a few minutes in.

A 1930s travel-poster night: sunburst rays behind a stepped skyline, a stepped double frame, Limelight capitals and Josefin Sans, everything flat and geometric. The moons are sleepy. Deco can be sleepy.

Six colours by sukinapan: dusk violet for the night and the rooftop, deep teal fading to cyan at the horizon, cream for the moons, peach for brass and blushes, coral for the box, Astrid's sparks and every NEW! sticker.

A wind-up music box waltzing in 3/4 in F major pentatonic over a harp, because it's 3 a.m. and the moons are asleep. A celesta joins when the crowd arrives, a warm pad when the gravity gets strong. Every flick, twinkle and ka-ching uses the same five notes.

BUT WAIT. Every upgrade is a product ('As seen on TV!', 'Set it and forget it!', 'Patented spring-loaded technology!'), the boxes keep coming whether you ordered them or not, leftover upgrades carry over at the same low price, and the fine print is load-bearing.
No calendar today. Just a roof, a box and a very well-read firework.

The Small Print Magnifier, the Commemorative Plate ('The Grand Finale, artist's impression') and the Extended Warranty ('covers everything except acts of gravity') all point at the last line of the manual: DO NOT EXCEED 99 MOONS PER SKY. MOONS MAY COLLAPSE (BEAUTIFULLY). RECOMMENDED USE: FINALE. Gravity was never the problem. It was the finale.

rolls.value: the number hits its cap and the world crunches
rolls.became: At 99 moons, the cap, the sky crunches: every moon spirals into every other one, and one enormous cracked moon hangs over the roof. Your last flick sends Dudley up into it, and he finally goes off, right in the middle, and all 99 moons come back down as stars. Astrid comes second. Astrid claps.

outro: Moon-in-a-Box is not available in stores. Results not typical. Operators are standing by.
